vignette:
For Samira, the world only makes sense in spreadsheets. In the neat columns and balanced ledgers of her work as an auditor, there is a predictable order, a logic that is both soothing and absolute. Every variance can be traced, every discrepancy reconciled. It is a stark contrast to the landscape of her own mind, a place she avoids with the same meticulousness she applies to her job.

She was twenty-five when she deployed, an idealistic Army linguist who believed her fluency in Arabic could be a bridge. She was proud of her heritage and proud of her new country, and she felt uniquely positioned to make a difference. For a time, she did. She translated during village elder meetings, helped de-escalate tense checkpoint standoffs, and felt a sense of purpose she had never known. The heat, the dust, the constant, low-grade tension—it all felt manageable, part of the mission.

The mission ended on a Tuesday afternoon on a road outside Fallujah. The memory doesn't arrive as a coherent thought, but as a sensory assault. It begins with the smell of diesel and hot dust, then the sudden, impossible brightness that bleached the sky white. The sound came next, a physical pressure that crushed the air from her lungs before her ears could even register the blast. Her Humvee, the third in the convoy, was thrown sideways into a ditch. She remembers the frantic shouting on the radio, then the silence. When she finally scrambled out, the vehicle ahead, the one carrying Sergeant Miller and two others, was a mangled, burning pyre against the blue sky. There was nothing to be done.

When she came home, the quiet was the strangest part. No generators humming, no distant gunfire, no calls to prayer. People thanked her for her service, their eyes filled with a pity she couldn't stand. She enrolled in college on the GI Bill, met a kind man named David, and built a new life. She chose accounting because it was precise. There was no ambiguity in numbers. She got married, bought a house, and landed a good job at a downtown firm. She told herself she was fine.

But the war had followed her home, a stowaway in her nervous system. She couldn't sleep through the night, waking up drenched in sweat, her heart hammering against her ribs from nightmares of fire and twisted metal. During the day, a car backfiring would send a jolt of pure terror through her, making her drop to a crouch behind her desk before she even knew why. She began mapping escape routes in restaurants and movie theaters, always needing to sit with her back to a wall, her eyes scanning every entrance.

David tried to be patient. He would hold her when she woke up screaming, but she would flinch from his touch. He couldn’t understand why she would erupt in rage over a misplaced set of keys, or why she would go silent for days, a wall of glass between them. She couldn’t explain it to him because she couldn’t explain it to herself. The love and joy she was supposed to feel were muted, distant signals from a foreign country. Eventually, the distance became a chasm, and David left. The divorce was just another variance she couldn't reconcile.

Now, at forty-five, her world has shrunk to the size of her apartment and her cubicle. Her work is her only sanctuary. She is known at her firm for her almost obsessive attention to detail, her ability to find the smallest error in thousands of lines of data. Her colleagues see it as dedication; they don’t see the hypervigilance that fuels it. They don’t know that she is not just checking for accounting fraud, but for threats—for the one detail out of place that signals impending disaster. Each balanced sheet is a small victory, a temporary imposition of order on a world that she knows, with absolute certainty, can dissolve into chaos in a flash of white light.
